newsitem.title: UK: Branson's balloon facing forced landing - agency.
newsitem.headline: Branson's balloon facing forced landing - agency.

text.p: British tycoon Richard Branson, attempting to become the first man to fly round the world in a balloon, will be forced to land soon due to a technical problem, Britain's Press Association news agency said on Wednesday.
The agency said it meant Branson's hopes of breaking "the last great aviation record left on earth" looked set to end in failure.
The balloon was expected to land in North Africa, possibly in Algeria or Libya, within the next few hours, said the agency.
"We can't tell you any more at this moment," it quoted a spokesman for Branson as saying.
The agency said Branson and co-pilots Per Lindstrand and Alex Ritchie, who lifted off from an air base near the Moroccan city of Marrakesh on Tuesday, were all well.

"This is one of the most magnificent adventures that anyone could have in their lifetime," Branson told reporters before lift-off. At Branson's mission control centre in London, a spokeswoman said the team spent the first few hours aloft getting to know how to handle the balloon, the Virgin Global Challenger.

They headed up into the jetstream they hoped would carry them across North Africa, Saudi Arabia, India, the South China Sea, the Pacific and the United States before landing in Britain in a 24,000-mile (38,600 km) trip expected to take between 14 and 21 days.
Branson has been racing against American balloonist Steve Fosset, who is planning a similar round-the-world attempt, launched from Switzerland.

Branson, flamboyant 46-year-old head of the Virgin group of companies, has launched an airline and products ranging from condoms to cola and pensions. He has previously crossed the Atlantic and Pacific by balloon.
His planned dawn takeoff had earlier been delayed by the complexities of inflating the giant balloon, a task taking over 12 hours.
Last January he had to cancel a previous attempt to fly round the globe from Marrakesh because of bad weather.
The record for the furthest flown by a manned balloon is 8,382 km (5,208 miles) from Japan to California, set by American Ben Abruzzo and three co-pilots in 1981.
